objective: Quadratic functions can be expressed in standard form (ax^2+bx+c) and factored form (a(x-r1)(x-r2)).；Key features of quadratic functions include x-intercepts (zeros), y-intercept, axis of symmetry, vertex, domain, range, and end behavior.；The reciprocal of a quadratic function, f(x)=1/(ax^2+bx+c), has vertical asymptotes at the zeros of the original quadratic.

Relate the graph of a quadratic to its reciprocal using sign intervals and extremum correspondence.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the factored form of the quadratic function f(x)=x²-5x+6?
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly converts from standard to factored form.
questions.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of polynomial functions, and make connections between the numeric, graphical, and algebraic representations of polynomial functions.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly tests conversion between forms, a key feature of polynomial functions.
questions.stemIntent: Assess ability to factor a quadratic from standard to factored form.
questions.commonMisconception: Sign errors in factors (e.g., using +2 and +3 instead of -2 and -3).

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: Check the signs: the constant term is +6, so the factors should multiply to +6 and sum to -5, meaning both factors are negative.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: This expands to x²+5x-6, not x²-5x+6.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: This expands to x²-5x-6, not x²-5x+6.

questions.stem: For the quadratic function f(x)=x²-4, the reciprocal function g(x)=1/(x²-4) has vertical asymptotes at:
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies vertical asymptotes from zeros of the original quadratic.
questions.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly tests understanding of vertical asymptotes in reciprocal rational functions.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding that zeros of the quadratic become vertical asymptotes of the reciprocal.
questions.commonMisconception: Thinking the reciprocal has zeros at the same x-values as the original quadratic.

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: The zeros of x²-4 are at x=2 and x=-2, not at 0 and 4.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: x²-4 has two zeros, not one.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: Since the denominator has zeros, vertical asymptotes exist at those x-values.

questions.stem: The reciprocal function g(x)=1/(x²-4) has x-intercepts at:
questions.successCriteria: Knows that reciprocal of a quadratic has no x-intercepts.
questions.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
questions.alignmentNote: Tests understanding that reciprocal functions have no x-intercepts.
questions.commonMisconception: Assuming it has x-intercepts, e.g., at zeros of the original.

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: Those are the vertical asymptotes, not x-intercepts. The reciprocal never equals zero.

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: Substituting x=0 gives g(0)=1/(-4)=-0.25, not zero.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: These are not relevant; the function is undefined at x=±2.

questions.stem: The horizontal asymptote of g(x)=1/(x²-4) is:
questions.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
questions.alignmentNote: Tests key feature of horizontal asymptote for reciprocal functions.
questions.stemIntent: Test knowledge that reciprocal quadratic has horizontal asymptote at y=0.
questions.commonMisconception: Thinking the horizontal asymptote is y=1 or determined by numerator degree.

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: The horizontal asymptote is found by comparing degrees; here numerator degree 0 < denominator degree 2, so HA is y=0.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: No; the reciprocal approaches 0 as x→±∞.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: Rational functions with denominator degree greater than numerator have HA at y=0.

questions.stem: Over the interval where f(x)=x²-4 is negative, g(x)=1/(x²-4) is:
questions.successCriteria: Relates sign of reciprocal to sign of original.
questions.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
questions.alignmentNote: Tests understanding of sign consistency between quadratic and its reciprocal.
questions.stemIntent: Check that reciprocal preserves sign of the original.
questions.commonMisconception: Thinking signs can differ (e.g., reciprocal becoming positive when original is negative).

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: If f(x) is negative, then 1/(negative) is also negative, not positive.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: The reciprocal cannot be zero; it approaches zero at infinities but isn't zero.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: It is defined as long as f(x) is not zero; negative intervals exclude zeros.

questions.stem: The quadratic f(x)=x²-4x+3 has a minimum value at x=2. The reciprocal function g(x)=1/(x²-4x+3) has at x=2:
questions.successCriteria: Correctly identifies that reciprocal has opposite type of extremum.
questions.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
questions.alignmentNote: Tests understanding of extremum correspondence between quadratic and reciprocal.
questions.stemIntent: Check knowledge that local maximum/minimum in quadratic gives local minimum/maximum in reciprocal.
questions.commonMisconception: Thinking both have same type of extremum (e.g., both minima).

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: The reciprocal has the opposite type of extremum: a minimum in the quadratic becomes a maximum in the reciprocal.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: At x=2, f(2)=-1, not zero, so no vertical asymptote.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: A hole occurs if the factor cancels; here the denominator is not zero at x=2.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly converts a quadratic function between standard and factored forms.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Confusing the conversion between standard and factored forms of a quadratic function.

miniLesson.explain: To convert a quadratic from standard form (ax^2+bx+c) to factored form (a(x-r1)(x-r2)), find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b when a=1. Write as (x + p)(x + q) with correct signs. For a≠1, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then factor by grouping.
miniLesson.example: Convert f(x)=x²-5x+6 to factored form. Find numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5: -2 and -3. Thus f(x)=(x-2)(x-3).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Factor pair: multiply to c, add to b.

reteachModules.trigger: Student thinks the reciprocal function has zeros at the same x-values as the original quadratic.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that the zeros of the quadratic become zeros of its reciprocal, rather than vertical asymptotes.

miniLesson.explain: When you take the reciprocal of a quadratic function, the zeros (x-intercepts) of the quadratic cause the reciprocal to become undefined because division by zero is not allowed. Instead of having a value at those points, the reciprocal function has vertical asymptotes, which are lines that the graph approaches but never touches. The reciprocal function never has x-intercepts because a fraction can only be zero if its numerator is zero, and here the numerator is 1.
miniLesson.example: Consider f(x)=x^2-4. Its zeros are x=2 and x=-2. The reciprocal g(x)=1/(x^2-4) has vertical asymptotes at x=2 and x=-2. Graphically, as x approaches 2 from the left, g(x) goes to negative infinity; from the right, to positive infinity. The reciprocal has no x-intercepts because 1 over something cannot be zero.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Zeros in the original become asymptotes in the reciprocal — they are 'no-go' vertical lines for the graph.

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify the vertical asymptotes of g(x)=1/(x^2-9).
Find the vertical asymptotes of g(x)=1/(x^2+2x-8).
guidedPractice.answer: Factor denominator: (x+4)(x-2), zeros at x=-4 and x=2, so asymptotes at x=-4 and x=2.

guidedPractice.prompt: The quadratic f(x)=x^2-6x+9 has a double root at x=3. Describe the behavior of its reciprocal g(x)=1/(x^2-6x+9) near x=3.
guidedPractice.answer: g(x) has a vertical asymptote at x=3. Since the factor is squared, both sides approach positive infinity (from left and right) because the quadratic is always non-negative and zero only at x=3.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly believes the reciprocal of a quadratic has x-intercepts.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think that the reciprocal function g(x)=1/(ax^2+bx+c) has x-intercepts, similar to the original quadratic. They may incorrectly set the reciprocal equal to zero and solve, not realizing that a fraction equals zero only when the numerator is zero.

miniLesson.explain: The reciprocal of a quadratic function, g(x)=1/f(x), has no x-intercepts because the numerator is constant (1). For a rational function to have an x-intercept, the numerator must be zero. Since 1 is never zero, the graph never crosses the x-axis. Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero, which are the x-intercepts of the original quadratic.
miniLesson.example: Consider f(x)=x^2-4. Its reciprocal is g(x)=1/(x^2-4). The x-intercepts of f are at x=2 and x=-2. For g, setting numerator=1 to zero gives no solution, so no x-intercepts. At x=2 and x=-2, g has vertical asymptotes.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: x-intercept means numerator zero. Reciprocal has numerator 1, so no x-intercepts. Zeros of original become asymptotes.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: The function g(x)=1/(x^2-9) has x-intercepts.
guidedPractice.answer: False. The numerator is 1, so g(x) can never be zero. It has no x-intercepts.

guidedPractice.prompt: Find the x-intercepts of g(x)=1/(x^2+2x+1), if any.
guidedPractice.answer: There are no x-intercepts because the numerator is 1. The denominator (x+1)^2 is zero at x=-1, but that is a vertical asymptote, not an x-intercept. So answer: no x-intercepts.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student claims that the reciprocal function g(x)=1/(x^2-5x+6) has x-intercepts at x=2 and x=3. Explain the error.
guidedPractice.answer: The student confused x-intercepts with vertical asymptotes. The original quadratic f(x)=x^2-5x+6 has zeros at x=2 and x=3. For g, these are vertical asymptotes because the denominator is zero. The reciprocal function has no x-intercepts because 1/(something) can never equal zero.

reteachModules.trigger: The student believes the horizontal asymptote of a reciprocal quadratic is something other than y=0.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Believing the horizontal asymptote of a reciprocal quadratic is something other than y=0.

miniLesson.explain: For a reciprocal quadratic function f(x)=1/(ax²+bx+c), the degree of the numerator (0) is less than the degree of the denominator (2). When the degree of the denominator is greater than the numerator, the horizontal asymptote is always y=0. As x → ±∞, the denominator grows without bound, so the fraction approaches 0.
miniLesson.example: Consider g(x)=1/(x²-4). As x → ±∞, x²-4 → ∞, so g(x) → 0. The graph approaches the line y=0 but never crosses it.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a fraction where the bottom is huge: the value becomes tiny, always approaching zero.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the horizontal asymptote of g(x)=1/(x²-9)?
Consider f(x)=x²-4. Its reciprocal is g(x)=1/(x²-4). As x→±∞, what does g(x) approach?
Explain why any reciprocal quadratic function has a horizontal asymptote at y=0.
guidedPractice.answer: Because the degree of the numerator (0) is less than the degree of the denominator (2). As x→±∞, the denominator grows without bound, making the fraction approach 0.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly selects an option indicating the reciprocal function can have a different sign than the original quadratic on the same interval.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Thinking the original quadratic and its reciprocal can have different signs (positive/negative) in the same interval.

miniLesson.explain: The original quadratic function and its reciprocal function always have the same sign in any interval where the quadratic is not zero. This is because the reciprocal of a positive number is positive, and the reciprocal of a negative number is negative.
miniLesson.example: Consider a quadratic function that is positive on an interval. Its reciprocal, 1 divided by a positive number, is also positive. Similarly, if the quadratic is negative, the reciprocal is negative.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Same sign, same team: the original and its reciprocal share the sign.

guidedPractice.prompt: If f(x) is positive on an interval, what is the sign of 1/f(x) on that interval?
If f(x) is negative on an interval, what is the sign of 1/f(x) on that interval?
A quadratic function f(x) has intervals where it is positive and intervals where it is negative. How can you determine the sign of its reciprocal on those intervals?
guidedPractice.answer: The reciprocal has the same sign as the quadratic on each interval where the quadratic is nonzero.

reteachModules.trigger: When asked about the relationship between a quadratic's extremum and its reciprocal's extremum, the student incorrectly thinks both have the same type (e.g., both minima or both maxima).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Confusing the correspondence between local maxima/minima of the quadratic and the reciprocal (e.g., thinking both are maxima).

miniLesson.explain: The local maximum or minimum (vertex) of a quadratic function corresponds to the opposite type of extremum in its reciprocal function. If the quadratic has a local minimum at a point, the reciprocal has a local maximum at that same x-coordinate, and vice versa. This happens because the reciprocal function 'flips' the shape: a valley becomes a peak and a peak becomes a valley.
miniLesson.example: Consider f(x)=x²-4x+3. This quadratic opens upward, so its vertex at x=2 is a minimum. The reciprocal g(x)=1/(x²-4x+3) will have a maximum at x=2. Indeed, g(2)=1/(-1)=-1, and nearby values are less than -1 (more negative) so it is a local maximum.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of flipping a smiley face (minimum) upside down: it becomes a frowny face (maximum). Extremum types swap between a function and its reciprocal.

guidedPractice.prompt: If a quadratic has a local maximum at x=3, what type of extremum does its reciprocal have at x=3?
For f(x)=-x²+2x+3, the vertex is at (1,4) and it is a maximum. Determine the nature of the extremum of g(x)=1/(-x²+2x+3) at x=1 and find its value.
guidedPractice.answer: g has a local minimum at x=1 with value g(1)=1/4=0.25

guidedPractice.prompt: A quadratic has zeros at x=1 and x=5 and a minimum at x=3. Sketch a rough graph of its reciprocal, labeling the type and location of the reciprocal's extremum.
guidedPractice.answer: The reciprocal has a vertical asymptote at x=1 and x=5, and a local maximum at x=3 (since the quadratic minimum corresponds to a reciprocal maximum). The reciprocal's graph is positive between asymptotes (if quadratic negative there, reciprocal positive? Actually need to check sign: quadratic minimum value is negative if it opens up and zeros at 1 and 5, so at x=3 f(3)=negative; reciprocal is negative there, but maximum means most negative? Wait careful: if quadratic has minimum negative, reciprocal has maximum (most positive? Let's clarify: For f(x)=a(x-1)(x-5) with a>0, at x=3 f(3)=a(2)(-2)=-4a <0, so reciprocal is negative. The reciprocal's maximum means it is the highest value, but still negative. So the maximum is at x=3, value negative. The correct answer: The reciprocal has a local maximum at x=3.

questions.rubric: Correct answer: \((x+5)(x-3)\) or equivalent with signs swapped.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about the reciprocal of a quadratic function?
options: The reciprocal has zeros at the same x-values as the quadratic.
The reciprocal has vertical asymptotes at the zeros of the quadratic.
The reciprocal has x-intercepts where the quadratic has vertical asymptotes.
The reciprocal has no vertical asymptotes.

questions.stem: Given the quadratic f(x)=x^2-4x+3, find the vertical asymptotes of its reciprocal g(x)=1/f(x).
questions.rubric: Factor f(x) to (x-1)(x-3). Zeros at x=1 and x=3. Vertical asymptotes at x=1 and x=3. Full credit (2 points) for both asymptotes correctly stated. Partial credit (1 point) if correct factoring but missing one asymptote. No credit otherwise.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select correct answer for question 1 and receive full rubric score (2 points) for question 2.

questions.stem: Does the function g(x) = 1/(x^2 - 4) have any x-intercepts?
options: No, because the numerator is 1, which can never be zero
No, because the denominator is always positive

questions.stem: Consider f(x) = x^2 - 5x + 6. Determine the x-intercepts of its reciprocal function g(x) = 1/(x^2 - 5x + 6). Explain your reasoning clearly.
questions.rubric: Student must state that g(x) has no x-intercepts because a fraction equals zero only when the numerator is zero, and here the numerator is 1 (never zero). They should note that the zeros of f (x=2 and x=3) are vertical asymptotes of g, not x-intercepts.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: What is the horizontal asymptote of the reciprocal quadratic function g(x)=1/(x^2-4)?
Explain why any reciprocal quadratic function f(x)=1/(ax^2+bx+c) has a horizontal asymptote at y=0.
questions.rubric: Student must state that the degree of the numerator is 0 and the degree of the denominator is 2, so the denominator grows much faster as x→∞, making the fraction approach 0. Accept any correct reasoning involving degrees or limit behavior.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: A quadratic function f(x) is positive on the interval (a, b). What is the sign of its reciprocal function g(x)=1/f(x) on the same interval?
Explain why the original quadratic function and its reciprocal function must have the same sign on any interval where the quadratic is nonzero.
questions.rubric: The reciprocal of a positive number is positive, and the reciprocal of a negative number is negative. Therefore, if f(x) is positive, 1/f(x) is positive; if f(x) is negative, 1/f(x) is negative. They share the same sign.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions answered correctly. Single choice must select 'Positive'. Open-ended must mention that reciprocal preserves sign (positive to positive, negative to negative).

questions.stem: Given the quadratic function f(x) = -2(x-4)^2 + 6, which has a maximum at x=4. What type of extremum does its reciprocal function g(x) = 1/f(x) have at x=4?
Explain why the type of extremum (maximum/minimum) of a quadratic function and its reciprocal are opposite at the same x-coordinate. Use the example f(x)=x^2-6x+8 in your explanation.
questions.rubric: Student identifies that the reciprocal 'flips' the shape: a minimum in the quadratic becomes a maximum in the reciprocal and vice versa, because the reciprocal function's graph is the reflection of the original's reciprocal values (e.g., near a minimum, the function values are small positive or negative, so reciprocal is large positive or negative respectively, creating a peak if the quadratic minimum is positive or a trough if negative? Actually careful: if quadratic has a minimum positive, reciprocal has a maximum positive? Wait: For f(x)=x^2-6x+8 = (x-3)^2 -1, vertex at (3,-1) is a minimum (value -1). Reciprocal g(x)=1/((x-3)^2-1). At x=3, g(3)=-1. For x near 3, (x-3)^2 is small positive, so denominator is -1+small, so g is negative and slightly less than -1? Let's compute: x=3.1, denominator 0.01-1=-0.99, g≈-1.01; x=2.9, similar. So g is more negative than -1 near 3, so at x=3, g is a local maximum because it is the highest (least negative) value near 3. So indeed minimum of f corresponds to maximum of g. Explanation should mention that as the quadratic increases from its vertex, its reciprocal decreases, and vice versa, leading to opposite extremum types.

diagnosisRules.condition: student picks wrong option on Q1 (targets err-quadratic-form-conversion)
student picks wrong option on Q2 (targets err-reciprocal-zeros-to-asymptotes)
student picks wrong option on Q3 (targets err-reciprocal-x-intercept)
student picks wrong option on Q4 (targets err-horizontal-asymptote)
student picks wrong option on Q5 (targets err-sign-consistency)
student picks wrong option on Q6 (targets err-extrema-correspondence)

nextActions: [err-quadratic-form-conversion] student picks wrong option on Q1 (targets err-quadratic-form-conversion): You need more practice converting between quadratic forms.
[err-reciprocal-zeros-to-asymptotes] student picks wrong option on Q2 (targets err-reciprocal-zeros-to-asymptotes): Remember: zeros of the quadratic become vertical asymptotes of the reciprocal.
[err-reciprocal-x-intercept] student picks wrong option on Q3 (targets err-reciprocal-x-intercept): The reciprocal of a quadratic has no x-intercepts because 1/(quadratic) can never be zero.
[err-horizontal-asymptote] student picks wrong option on Q4 (targets err-horizontal-asymptote): The horizontal asymptote of a reciprocal quadratic is always y=0.
[err-sign-consistency] student picks wrong option on Q5 (targets err-sign-consistency): The original quadratic and its reciprocal have the same sign in any interval.
[err-extrema-correspondence] student picks wrong option on Q6 (targets err-extrema-correspondence): A local maximum in the quadratic corresponds to a local minimum in the reciprocal, and vice versa.

cards.question: Which of the following is the factored form of the quadratic function f(x)=x²-5x+6?
cards.diagnosis: Assess ability to factor a quadratic from standard to factored form.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
Check the signs: the constant term is +6, so the factors should multiply to +6 and sum to -5, meaning both factors are negative.
This expands to x²+5x-6, not x²-5x+6.
This expands to x²-5x-6, not x²-5x+6.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly converts from standard to factored form.
cards.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of polynomial functions, and make connections between the numeric, graphical, and algebraic representations of polynomial functions.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly tests conversion between forms, a key feature of polynomial functions.
cards.commonMisconception: Sign errors in factors (e.g., using +2 and +3 instead of -2 and -3).

cards.question: For the quadratic function f(x)=x²-4, the reciprocal function g(x)=1/(x²-4) has vertical asymptotes at:
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding that zeros of the quadratic become vertical asymptotes of the reciprocal.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
The zeros of x²-4 are at x=2 and x=-2, not at 0 and 4.
x²-4 has two zeros, not one.
Since the denominator has zeros, vertical asymptotes exist at those x-values.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies vertical asymptotes from zeros of the original quadratic.
cards.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly tests understanding of vertical asymptotes in reciprocal rational functions.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking the reciprocal has zeros at the same x-values as the original quadratic.

cards.question: The reciprocal function g(x)=1/(x²-4) has x-intercepts at:
misconceptions: Those are the vertical asymptotes, not x-intercepts. The reciprocal never equals zero.
Substituting x=0 gives g(0)=1/(-4)=-0.25, not zero.
✓ 正确
These are not relevant; the function is undefined at x=±2.
cards.successCriteria: Knows that reciprocal of a quadratic has no x-intercepts.
cards.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
cards.alignmentNote: Tests understanding that reciprocal functions have no x-intercepts.
cards.commonMisconception: Assuming it has x-intercepts, e.g., at zeros of the original.

cards.question: The horizontal asymptote of g(x)=1/(x²-4) is:
cards.diagnosis: Test knowledge that reciprocal quadratic has horizontal asymptote at y=0.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
The horizontal asymptote is found by comparing degrees; here numerator degree 0 < denominator degree 2, so HA is y=0.
No; the reciprocal approaches 0 as x→±∞.
Rational functions with denominator degree greater than numerator have HA at y=0.
cards.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
cards.alignmentNote: Tests key feature of horizontal asymptote for reciprocal functions.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking the horizontal asymptote is y=1 or determined by numerator degree.

cards.question: Over the interval where f(x)=x²-4 is negative, g(x)=1/(x²-4) is:
cards.diagnosis: Check that reciprocal preserves sign of the original.
misconceptions: If f(x) is negative, then 1/(negative) is also negative, not positive.
✓ 正确
The reciprocal cannot be zero; it approaches zero at infinities but isn't zero.
It is defined as long as f(x) is not zero; negative intervals exclude zeros.
cards.successCriteria: Relates sign of reciprocal to sign of original.
cards.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
cards.alignmentNote: Tests understanding of sign consistency between quadratic and its reciprocal.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking signs can differ (e.g., reciprocal becoming positive when original is negative).

cards.question: The quadratic f(x)=x²-4x+3 has a minimum value at x=2. The reciprocal function g(x)=1/(x²-4x+3) has at x=2:
cards.diagnosis: Check knowledge that local maximum/minimum in quadratic gives local minimum/maximum in reciprocal.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
The reciprocal has the opposite type of extremum: a minimum in the quadratic becomes a maximum in the reciprocal.
At x=2, f(2)=-1, not zero, so no vertical asymptote.
A hole occurs if the factor cancels; here the denominator is not zero at x=2.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly identifies that reciprocal has opposite type of extremum.
cards.ossdExpectation: Identify and describe some key features of the graphs of rational functions, and represent rational functions graphically.
cards.alignmentNote: Tests understanding of extremum correspondence between quadratic and reciprocal.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking both have same type of extremum (e.g., both minima).
